claims.text: The low hardness and strength of equimolar CoCrFeNiTi arise from reduced valence electron concentration caused by Ti addition.
Reduced valence electron concentration weakens average metallic bonding.
Weaker average metallic bonding lowers the critical resolved shear stress for dislocation motion.
The comparator is equimolar CoCrFeNi in a single-phase solid-solution state with a grain size of 20–50 µm.
Adding Ti in an amount that produces equimolar CoCrFeNiTi can retain a single-phase solid solution under the proposed processing.
The CoCrFeNi and CoCrFeNiTi specimens can be prepared with the same processing and grain size.
Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has a lower composition-derived average VEC than equimolar CoCrFeNi.
Reduced VEC decreases lattice friction, including Peierls stress.
Reduced lattice friction decreases CRSS and permits dislocation glide at lower applied stress.
CoCrFeNiTi is predicted to have 15–25% lower hardness than CoCrFeNi under matched conditions.
The predicted hardness changes from approximately 200 HV for CoCrFeNi to approximately 150–170 HV for CoCrFeNiTi.
CoCrFeNiTi is predicted to have 15–25% lower yield strength than CoCrFeNi under matched conditions.
The predicted yield strength changes from approximately 300 MPa for CoCrFeNi to approximately 225–255 MPa for CoCrFeNiTi.
Equimolar CoCrFeNi has a baseline hardness of approximately 200 HV under the proposed testing conditions.
Equimolar CoCrFeNi has a baseline yield strength of approximately 300 MPa under the proposed testing conditions.
Restricting total strain to below 2% avoids significant work-hardening effects.
The magnitude of the influence of VEC on CRSS in high-entropy alloys is not fully quantified.
